h1: Bringing a foreign beer brand to India
title: Bringing a Foreign Beer Brand to India | Craft Beer School
desc: How a foreign beer brand can reach India: import, contract brew or licence the brand. See what state rules, customs and distribution mean for each.
teaser: A beer that sells well at home meets a different set of rules, tastes and temperatures in India.
standfirst: A foreign beer brand can enter India by importing finished beer, brewing under contract or licensing the brand to a local brewer. This guide compares the three and lists what to check first.
sections:
Importing means shipping finished beer from your brewery. You keep full control of the product. Cost and shelf life are the issues, since shipping takes weeks and warm containers harm beer.

Contract brewing means an Indian brewery makes the beer to your recipe. Freshness improves and cost per bottle can fall. You depend on a host. Quality control becomes your main task.

Licensing means an Indian company brews and sells under your brand and pays you for it. You carry less cash risk. You also hand much of the brand's treatment to someone else.

Many brands start with import to test demand and move to contract brewing when volume justifies it.

Alcohol is a state subject. Each state controls licences, excise duty, brand registration, pricing and who may sell. These differ between states and change. In some states imported beer needs a separate route and carries different duties from domestic beer. Several states, including Bihar and Gujarat, have prohibition. Check the current rules for any state you plan to enter.

Imports also involve central customs duty and import registration at the border. Labels must meet central labelling rules and may need state-specific approval. Work with a licensing adviser and a lawyer. This guide gives the shape of the process, not legal advice.
Fit the beer to the conditions

India is hot. Cold chain is patchy. Beer shipped in warm containers or stored in warm shops can go stale within weeks. Pasteurised or well-protected packaging and a short route to the customer help. Heavily hopped beers lose aroma quickly in heat.

Consider the style too. Light lagers and wheat beers sit comfortably with Indian food and weather. Strong or very bitter beers need a clear audience. Do some market research before you decide what to bring. Our guide on market research in India for a foreign drinks brand explains how.

The state decides how beer gets to the customer. In some states a state corporation buys and sells. In others private distributors and retailers hold licences. Bars, restaurants and shops each follow their own rules. Our guide to craft beer distribution models describes the main patterns.

Price rises along the chain through duties and margins, so the shelf price can sit well above the ex-brewery price. Work the numbers state by state from official sources and your adviser, not from a global average.

Register your trademark in India early. Names that work abroad may be taken, or may mean something unintended in an Indian language. Check before you print labels. Brand and label registration with the state excise authority is a separate step in many states.

Plan the story for Indian drinkers as well. Craft beer is still young in India. Customers need a reason to try a new name.

Before you commit to a route, run a small test. A limited import into one chosen state, or a tasting with trade buyers in a licensed venue, tells you more than a desk study. Treat the test as research and record what buyers say about taste, price and packaging.

Look at the answers honestly. If buyers like the beer but balk at the price, contract brewing may fix that. If they are lukewarm on the taste, no route will help until the product changes.

Keep the first move small enough that you can walk away from it.

Write down what a good result looks like before you start: the number of buyers who reorder, the price they accept and the feedback on taste. Without that, any outcome can be read as success.
faqs: Is importing the simplest way to start?
It can be quick for a test, but duties, state rules and shelf life make it costly at volume. Many brands test by importing and then move to local production.
Can I sell the same beer in every state?
Not automatically. Licences, duties and registration differ between states. Some states prohibit alcohol.
Do I need a local partner?
Most foreign brands find one useful for licences, distribution and market knowledge. The choice of partner matters more than the speed of finding one.
